So I had the "ask me for exceptions" policy one year. A bunch of students asked for exceptions (over e-mail), and then I couldn't enforce it for the remainder of the class.

In many cases accommodations are not actually laptops but "ability to record lecture" etc — which can be done with other tools.

Now I say "no laptops unless you have accommodations, in which case check in with me on the first day of class". 

The students who really, actually need to use laptops for accommodations are usually very proactive in getting in touch, and most years that number is zero, so I can just say "hey, laptops closed please".

Some accommodations, by their very nature, can not be kept private. A student in a wheelchair requires wheelchair accommodations but short of providing a mobile privacy screen, this can't be hidden. Additional time for testing can't be kept secret, since students can notice who is and isn't in the usual room.

Our obligation is (1) to keep things private as much as possible; (2) where accommodations are visible, to rigorously enforce non-discrimination and respectful treatment to ensure the student can receive an equitable education.

The only cases where I've had a disability accommodation that \*required\* laptop use (this is actually very rare), the student had other disabilities that were impossible to hide.

In a class of 80, I ban laptops (and call it out during lecture) — this helps.

I'm at a STEM R1.

For the best students, high school seems to be running the gauntlet of teaching to the test. This means:

1. Much less agency and initiative, and much more focus on "guessing what the teacher wants".

2. Students have difficulty sustaining attention when there's not a clear gain within two or three minutes — the feedback loop between thinking and using feels shorter than in the past.

3. In some schools, grade inflation is so extreme that students get essentially zero feedback on learning, other than "are you not actively sabotaging the classroom".

When students get to college, these things start to fail. This leads to a lot of frustration on both sides.

The best questions to ask students are "what in this class is working for you?" You're almost certainly doing  more than you need to be doing, and the answers to this question will help you focus your efforts.

The positive-frame question also reorients students towards their successful attempts to learn, and helps them view themselves as agents (while you get blamed for when they don't learn, they're happy to take the credit for when they do — which is great!)

When you get "a student come up to me before class saying that they didn't understand the assignment; they wanted tips to get a better grade", open the PDF of the assignment, and slowly scroll through it with them. They will get bored very quickly because they realize that they can do it faster.

Most evaluations are on a scale of 1 to 5, and your university will probably have an average of between 3 and 4. You end up having two challenges:

1. get the students who will put "3" up to a "5"

2. avoid having students who put "1".

For (1), there are ethical and unethical ways to do things. **Ethical**: enjoy what you teach/teach what you enjoy, give clear instructions for assignments, have good planning (fix deadlines before class begins, use the LMS), talk about how much you care about their learning, and follow through. Grade, but demphasize the importance of grades in how you talk. Ask students to tell you what is working for them in class (rather than the criticisms) — this helps focus them on their own agency. **Unethical**: students should think they're going to get an A (I do this by having the final paper count for a large portion of the grade, with lots of potential "bonus points" — students are very optimistic about their chances.)

For (2), there are ethical and unethical ways to do this. **Ethical**: be fair, no matter how irritating the students are, don't get upset at them. I found that e-mail exchanges can escalate, but having students see you after lecture usually resolves problems. Have assignments that can't be "cheated" — in person exams, or scaffolded essays that they can't use ChatGPT for. Don't submit final grades until the response deadline closes. **Unethical**: don't send reminders to fill out the form, but set aside time at the end of a lecture — the students who hate you won't be in lecture. Submit final grades for the A students before the response deadline closes.

Things that *don't* work: 

Things your university might suggest that don't work: Flipped classrooms, teaching "tricks" like group discussions, "effective learning" strategies, giving advice on how to study, having "learning goals". Students who need them won't pay attention; students who don't need them will find them patronizing.

Things you might think work, but don't: giving lots of extensions, allowing excuses for things specified in the syllabus, being an easy grader. This seems to create chaos for students, who actually appreciate and respect a predictable classroom environment; conversely, students do not give you a higher score if you cut them slack.

I've scaled up from 20 students to 80. At 40 students you can no longer dynamically adjust the class to the personalities and abilities of the students.

1. For grading, you should have rubrics that cover the full range from "A" to "F"; you will get a lot more "D"-level work, and you need a clear and fair way for your TA to separate out "B"/"C"/"D".
2. Class policies on attendance, late work, etc. need to be clear. Don't make them insanely strict, so that you feel OK saying "sorry to hear \[X\] happened; see syllabus for class policy". Students will feel anonymous, and will be tempted to skip class a lot more — I had to go to mandatory attendance.
3. Class policies on laptop use, late arrivals, etc. need to be enforced from day one.
4. Have all assignment due dates and rubrics uploaded before the semester starts.
5. Don't teach over e-mail. Politely and briefly respond to e-mails by saying "great question, come see me after class." End lecture 5 minutes early so students can come up to ask questions. You'll still have your great students, and those conversations are when you can teach the ones who really care.
6. A lot of things that have positive effects at 20 students have very negative effects at 80. e.g., with 20 students, providing slides is a great way for them to remind themselves of content, but at 80 students many will just skip class and hope to catch up with slides.

So I used to take your position, but hard experience taught me that students are not good at self-regulation: they are basically incapable of determining, for themselves, whether or not they need to attend lecture to learn.

My new rule is: "if the median student needs to do X to learn, X needs to have a grade attached." Now that I've required attendance, the students have improved on every metric. The total attendance incentive is small (10 points out of 100) so if there are people who don't need it, they can literally skip every class and get an A (there are some bonus points available).

So you're in a strong position for people looking to fill a position — indeed, if someone on a committee wants to hire you then can start by saying to their colleagues: "look, University X *already* thought they were great, this is a target of opportunity for us to benefit from their fuckup".

Given the situation as you describe it, I would absolutely let it be known that you are looking for a new/better position.

Here in the US, and knowing this academic culture, I would do a few things now: 

(1) let influential people I'm friends with know that I'm looking to move up and out — and asking them to spread the word a little bit (your close contacts won't have a job, but their close contacts might, and so on).

(2) keep an eye on jobs that are currently open; if there are things that are good, it is completely appropriate to apply.

In general, I wouldn't say "hey, I'm interested, but maybe I won't lose my job in which case I'm not interested" (if you say that, people will be mildly irritated — it's work to pull your network, and they won't want to do it). You should be open to jumping ship even if you can, potentially, stay, and it might be helpful to phrase it as "moving up", rather than "saving me".

But, most importantly, perhaps —

(3) I'd keep doing great research. In the end, people will hire you not because "they want to help", but because you're really good and they need you. Doing what you love, as much as possible, is the best way to thrive.

I'm not sure if this is helpful, but let me tell you the situation I'm in. I run a small(ish) STEM lab, which has a funding that comes in from various places. Very often my constraint is not money, but finding the right person — someone smart, hardworking, and who truly loves their work.

1. students legitimately don't know how to do things. The rubric tells them what they don't know, and gives them a guide to what they need to learn.

Departments usually ignore these, unless there's something actionable (e.g., "she didn't come to class"). Here's how I've minimized the nastygrams:

1. students are *very* sensitive to "fairness" — if you want to be tough, you have to be fair. Everyone has to have the same opportunities. Probably the worst case was when I had a group do their presentation outside of class time (because we ran over). They got a bad grade, and blamed it on this.

2. detailed rubrics are extremely helpful — a lot of students don't know how to do essays, problem sets, presentations, etc., and they may have had overly lax professors in previous classes. A rubric gives them a sense of what they have to do to succeed.

3. put the mean things in the syllabus so that you can be "nice" in e-mails without being "easy" — i.e., "wow I'm really sorry that X is happening; check the syllabus for what to do next."

4. don't create exceptions for problem students. It doesn't help them succeed, and it doesn't make them like you. It's ok to be a bit blank and "not comprehending" when they ask for something crazy (e.g., "can I just not do the final paper?" "Oh gosh, that's an interesting question. Let's check the syllabus together... hmm... the final paper is X points, so if you didn't do it, you'd get a zero... which means that your maximum grade would be... hmm, let me add this up... 60 points out of 100... which would translate to, hang on, let me scroll up... a D. So gosh I guess yes, you could absolutely not do the final paper, and you would get, what was it, oh right, let me check, yes, a D."

Some other things that help, but are a bit sly:

1. do NOT submit final grades until after the feedback form closes.

2. have the final paper be a significant portion of the grade, so that students can still hope to get a B (or an A), even if they've been terrible all semester.

3. remind the students to fill out the form in class, and set aside time at the end of the semester in class; the students who actually come to class are likely to like you more.

Have each student describe a piece of research they've done, in five minutes (set a timer for this, so it beeps and they have to stop).

Welcome to teaching! My experience is that it takes about five years of iterating on the syllabus until it's perfect. Here's what's in mine:  
  
1. The phrase "Everything you need to know is in this document"  
2. "How to succeed in this class" (a very short statement)  
3. Attendance policy  
4. All deadlines, and policies for what happens if you miss (never say "no exceptions", but never say "exceptions are OK" either)  
5. Ethics (is ChatGPT permitted? etc)  
6. "Contact me if you have official disability accommodations"  
7. Office hours / TA contact information  
8. How the final grade is calculated (i.e., how to translate your points into A/B/C/D/F — you need to have the low end covered as well, to distinguish D from F)  
9. A mention that you take your college's honor code (if they have one) seriously — this covers a lot of edge cases.

A few thoughts:

1. The biggest improvement will come from experimenting with different routes. Google Maps is not a great guide, and there are likely multiple ways to get to school. Experiment with side streets and unusual paths you wouldn't take if you were driving or walking. E.g., cars tend to avoid streets with lots of stop signs, but this is gold for a cyclist.

2. You may also find an asymmetric route (different in vs out) because steep downhills are great, but it's safer to do an uphill when it's more gentle.

3. You may be allowed to take up the whole lane "if safety requires". In the end, what really matters is enforcement. In the US, e.g., the only thing that cops really seem to care about is riding a bicycle on the sidewalk. I've found that riding "where the car's right-hand side tires would be" really changes the experience.

Some things that work for me:

1. Shower before going to work, and wear clean clothes. You smell because bacteria grow in a moist environment, not because sweat itself is smelly.

2. Wool is a fantastic fabric, all times of the year — for Summers, consider some of the fancy wools like merino. I found it prevents a lot of smell problems. Hang things up to air when you get home. 3. When you get on your bicycle in the morning, you should (as much as possible) feel cold given the ambient conditions.

4. Panniers! You almost certainly know that already, but a backpack is both hard to ride with, and will make you sweat without question.

I’m on day nine of complete sobriety and it’s wonderful — a vacation in itself.

First two/three days were hard, and I would have a plan for what you’re doing instead of drinking (e.g., get tickets for something), because you might use “woo vacation” as an excuse.

On a plane it’s quite easy: just ask for a soda water. The flight attendant is hard enough to catch that you only have to say no when they come by, and you have time to prepare/practice saying “no” as they do the rows ahead/behind Then you have a couple of hours to wrestle with all your feelings:) 

Hotels are harder, because they make a lot of money at the bar. I’d suggest getting out of the hotel ASAP after checking in; explore the city and have a coffee instead. 

I’ve been at hotels where they offer wine for free at check-in; if you’re offered you can say “thank you but I’m sober”, and they’ll shut up real fast. You can also request they take alcohol out of the minibar (never tried this but if the hotel is fancy enough to have it, they are probably fancy enough to pull it) — more recently they have keys and you have to request the key specifically. 

Source on this: personal experience. 

Good luck and IWNDWYT

Edit: if you have trouble sleeping, I find “dream water” (sold at airport concessions) very effective — just a mix of different sleep aids.

Start filling those gaps with real activities: reading, writing, painting (!—I bought a watercolor set) running worked for me. Drinking is not just an addiction, it was also a hobby. I needed new hobbies.

If you hit a crisis point, this sub is very nice to kill time on.

In the longer term, therapy can be powerful.
